title: Testing and Quality
eyebrow: Confidence in change · Turn expected behavior into repeatable evidence
summary: Start with a small behavior that can break, write an observable check for it, then expand into test boundaries, assertions, doubles, browser interaction, coverage, flaky failures, and a maintainable verification pipeline.
prerequisites: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript is helpful because examples use JavaScript behavior.
Node.js and Package Management is helpful because test commands run through project scripts.
React is helpful for the browser-interaction example, but the testing model does not depend on React.
learningOutcomes: Choose a test boundary from the behavior and failure risk rather than from a preferred test label.
Write tests whose setup, action, observable result, and cleanup make failures diagnosable.
Use doubles, coverage, and continuous integration without mistaking them for proof that every behavior is correct.

heroVisual.title: A test checks a behavior at a chosen boundary
heroVisual.caption: The smallest useful boundary is not always the smallest piece of code: choose the layer that can observe the behavior a user or dependent system needs.

nodes.label: Example input
nodes.detail: A known request, value, click, or stored state starts the scenario.

nodes.label: System boundary
nodes.detail: The test chooses a function, module, service, or rendered interface to exercise.

nodes.label: Observable result
nodes.detail: The assertion checks returned data, a state change, a request, or visible output.

nodes.label: Evidence
nodes.detail: A repeatable pass or failure helps decide whether the change is safe.

sections.title: 1. Start with a behavior a person can observe
sections.summary: A useful test names the input, action, and result before choosing a framework.

blocks.text: Suppose a checkout form refuses an empty email address. The behavior is more useful than the implementation detail: given an empty field, submitting the form should show an error and should not send an order request. A test turns that expectation into a repeatable scenario.

items.title: Arrange
items.explanation: Create the smallest known starting state, such as an empty email field.
items.result: The scenario starts with controlled input.

items.title: Act
items.explanation: Perform the same action that matters, such as submitting the form.

items.title: Assert
items.explanation: Check the observable result: the validation message is present and the request was not sent.
items.result: The test records whether the expected behavior occurred.

items.title: Clean up
items.explanation: Restore timers, files, servers, or other shared resources so the next test starts independently.
items.result: The next test gets an independent starting state.

blocks.prompt: If a test only asserts that a private helper was called, does it prove that the user saw the required validation message?
blocks.explanation: The helper call is an implementation detail. The visible message and prevented request are the behavior the scenario needs to protect.

sections.title: 2. Choose the boundary from the question the test must answer
sections.summary: Different boundaries trade speed, isolation, and realism.

rows: Unit
Does one focused piece calculate the expected result for its inputs?
Fast and isolated, but it can miss wiring between pieces.
Integration
Do several real pieces collaborate through their boundary?
Finds configuration and data-shape problems, but needs more setup.
End to end
Can a person complete the important journey through the running system?
Most realistic, but slower and more sensitive to environment failures.
blocks.caption: Use the narrowest boundary that can answer the real question; combine boundaries for important behavior.

blocks.text: A unit test is not automatically better because it is fast. If the failure is caused by a form, router, request handler, and response working together, an integration test may provide clearer evidence. End-to-end tests belong around a few high-value journeys, not every internal branch.

blocks.title: Test behavior, not a frozen implementation
blocks.body: Prefer stable outputs and user-visible effects. Assertions tied to private names or exact markup can fail during a safe refactor and teach the team to avoid useful change.

sections.title: 3. Keep assertions precise, and isolate only what you control
sections.summary: Assertions explain what failed; test doubles control an external boundary when using the real dependency would be slow, unsafe, or nondeterministic.

blocks.explanation: The test supplies a known token, calls the public operation, and checks the stable outcome. It does not assert which private parser or branch produced the result.

blocks.text: A test double stands in for another component. A stub supplies a controlled answer, a spy records that a call happened, and a mock usually combines configured behavior with interaction expectations. Use a double at a boundary such as a payment provider when a real call would charge money or depend on the network. Keep the real database or browser in tests whose purpose is to verify that boundary.

blocks.prompt: Should a retry test wait for a real network timeout when the question is whether the client retries twice?
blocks.explanation: A controlled boundary can fail immediately and deterministically. A separate integration test can verify the actual transport behavior without making the core retry test slow and flaky.

sections.title: 4. Exercise interfaces through the same controls a person uses
sections.summary: Browser tests are strongest when they use semantic controls and observe the resulting interface.

blocks.text: For a React form, render the form, find its label and submit button by their accessible roles or names, enter a value, and check the message a person can perceive. This verifies component wiring, state updates, and semantics together. It also catches a missing label that a test querying a private component variable would miss.

items.title: Start clean
items.explanation: Render the form with no saved state and wait for only the work the scenario needs.
items.result: The interface has a known initial state.

items.title: Use the interface
items.explanation: Locate the named input, enter the invalid value, and press the semantic submit control.
items.result: The same controls a person uses trigger validation.

items.title: Observe the result
items.explanation: Assert the error is exposed and focus or status behavior is correct where the user needs it.
items.result: The test checks the accessible outcome.

items.title: Cover the recovery
items.explanation: Correct the value and assert that the error clears and the success path becomes available.
items.result: The scenario proves recovery, not only rejection.

blocks.title: Do not hide asynchronous work
blocks.body: A test that asserts before a request or render settles can pass by accident or fail intermittently. Wait for the observable state, then assert it; do not add arbitrary sleeps to guess when work is finished.

sections.title: 5. Read coverage and failures as investigation clues
sections.summary: A green suite is evidence for the scenarios it exercises, not a proof of correctness.

blocks.text: Coverage reports show which lines, branches, functions, or statements ran. High coverage can still miss a wrong assertion, an invalid test input, or a production configuration. Low coverage identifies unexamined paths; decide whether the missing path changes a user outcome or failure risk before chasing a percentage.

rows: Fails only after another test
Shared state, fake timers, environment variables, or incomplete cleanup
Run the test alone and in a randomized order; remove the shared dependency.
Passes locally but fails in CI
Runtime version, timezone, filesystem, network, or resource assumptions
Compare the environments and capture the first failing assertion and logs.
Times out
Unresolved promise, server lifecycle, or wait condition
Inspect pending work and use a bounded wait for the expected observable result.
Snapshot changes everywhere
Broad serialized output or a real shared behavior change
Review the diff; do not update snapshots without understanding each changed behavior.
blocks.caption: Diagnose the stage that produced the symptom before changing the test.

sections.title: 6. Make the useful checks repeatable in development and CI
sections.summary: A quality pipeline gives fast local feedback and a clean, reproducible release gate.

blocks.explanation: Named scripts give people and continuous integration the same commands. The test command checks behavior; type checking and the build check different failure classes. One green result must not be treated as the others.

blocks.title: A maintainable test change
items: Name the behavior and failure risk in the test.
Use independent setup and deterministic inputs.
Assert the result that a user or dependent system relies on.
Keep external calls controlled unless the test is specifically an integration check.
Run the focused test first, then the repository gate.
Remove obsolete tests only when the protected behavior is deliberately retired.

blocks.text: Test-driven development (TDD) is one workflow: write a failing example, make the smallest change that passes it, then refactor while the example remains green. It can clarify a contract, but it is not a requirement that every change begin with a unit test. The durable requirement is evidence matched to risk.

glossary.definition: A check that compares an observed result with an expected condition and reports a failure when they differ.
Known setup data or resources used to make a test scenario repeatable.
A controlled replacement for a dependency used to isolate or observe a test boundary.
A previously working behavior that stops working after a change.
A measurement of which recorded code locations or paths a test suite executed.
A test whose result changes between runs without a relevant product change.
Test-driven development: a workflow of failing example, passing implementation, and refactoring.
